Volume 12 · Chapter 10

Structural estimation and economic mechanisms

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v12-c09

By the endConnect economic models to data and distinguish calibration from identified estimation.

Volume 12 · Chapter 10

Structural estimation and economic mechanisms

A firm replaces equipment, buyers respond to a tax, and households adopt a service whose usefulness depends on other users. A regression can summarize each outcome. A structural model additionally says which preferences, technologies, information and equilibrium conditions produced it. The extra structure can support a policy experiment, but the data may not identify that structure, and the policy may change the very mechanism held fixed in the calculation.

Capability. Derive a model-to-data map; distinguish identification, normalization, calibration and a statistical projection; account for simulation sharing and numerical error; estimate through auxiliary moments; differentiate a finite dynamic model; and report an equilibrium set when the selection rule is unknown. Six original synthetic cases separate mathematical conclusions from empirical claims.

Prerequisites. Chapter 9 distinguishes the law of a stochastic process from a convenient covariance description. Recall the contraction and implicit-function tools in Volume 2, Chapter 10, compact extremum and iid limit arguments in Chapter 1, instrumental variables and minimum distance in Chapter 3, and likelihood targets and sandwich inference in Chapter 4. We prove the particular simulation and equilibrium results used here; a citation to a dynamic model does not supply a general dependent-data estimation theorem.

1. A mechanism, an observable map and a target

Let θ be a finite vector of primitive parameters in a declared domain Θ. A maintained model specifies behavior, the distribution of shocks, what agents know, the observation rule and, where needed, equilibrium selection. These components generate an observable probability law Pθ. Identification means Pθ=Pθ₀ implies θ=θ₀ within Θ. If estimation uses only a population moment map m(θ), moment identification instead requires m(θ)=m(θ₀) to have a unique admissible solution. Discarding information can destroy identification. A full-rank local derivative supports a local inverse; it does not exclude a distant second solution.

Normalization chooses units or an observationally redundant location. Calibration fixes an input using an external number or a maintained restriction. Estimation supplies a data-dependent rule and a sampling law. A calibrated value may be scientifically defensible, but fixing it does not prove the current data identify it. Under misspecification, an estimator can converge precisely to a projection or pseudo-true parameter that does not describe the actual technology or preferences.

A counterfactual changes a stated intervention while preserving specified primitives. This invariance is a substantive hypothesis. A fitted baseline does not establish that tastes, information, constraints, shock distributions or equilibrium selection survive the intervention. Price and quantity below are in synthetic currency and output units; costs share the price units. Choice utilities later use a normalized shock scale, with no supplied conversion into money.

A compact extremum argument, with its missing step made visible

Suppose Θ is compact, Q is continuous with unique maximizer θ₀, and supθ∈Θ|QN(θ)−Q(θ)|→p0. Let θ̂N satisfy QN(θ̂N)≥sup QN−aN, where aN→p0. For any ε>0 whose complement Kε={θ:‖θ−θ₀‖≥ε} is nonempty, compactness and uniqueness give an attained separation

δε=Q(θ₀)−maxKεQ(θ)>0.

On the event that the uniform error and aN are each below δε/3, every θ in Kε has QN(θ₀)−QN(θ)>δε/3 and cannot be the selected approximate maximizer. The event has probability tending to one. Thus θ̂N→pθ₀. If Kε is empty the assertion is immediate. Continuity of QN ensures an exact maximum exists; it does not show that a particular optimizer found it. Pointwise convergence alone does not provide the uniform error used in this proof. The finite and scalar-noise constructions below establish that error directly.

2. Equilibrium variation can identify different slopes

Worked case 1: a supply shift, a demand shift and a tax

In a synthetic population, W,Z,U,V are independent fair signs, each equal to −1 or 1. W shifts demand, Z shifts supply, and U,V are equation shocks. Demand and supply clear at one price:

Q=10+W−2P+U,   Q=1+P−Z+V.

There are 16 equally likely atoms. Solving the two equations, rather than treating price as externally fixed, gives

P=3+(W+Z+U−V)/3,
Q=4+(W−2Z+U+2V)/3.

Thus E(P,Q)=(3,4). Independence and centering give Cov(Z,U)=0 and Cov(W,V)=0. The excluded cost instrument yields (Cov(Z,P),Cov(Z,Q))=(1/3,−2/3), so the demand coefficient on price is −2. The excluded demand instrument yields (Cov(W,P),Cov(W,Q))=(1/3,1/3), identifying the supply coefficient 1. The nonzero denominators establish relevance in this population. The exclusions come from the stipulated model, not from these covariance ratios.

Ordinary least squares does not recover those slopes. After removing W and an intercept, price has residual (Z+U−V)/3 and quantity has residual (−2Z+U+2V)/3. Their covariance is −1/3 and price variance is 1/3, producing coefficient −1. Removing Z instead gives residuals (W+U−V)/3 and (W+U+2V)/3, whose covariance is zero, producing 0. The disturbance enters the market-clearing price. More observations from this law do not remove that endogeneity.

A unit tax t changes the producer receipt to P−t. Holding all primitives and shock laws fixed gives Pt=P+t/3 and Qt=Q−2t/3. At t=1, mean price and quantity are (10/3,10/3). Consumer price rises by one third; producer net price falls by two thirds. These are consequences of the maintained tax experiment, not a causal claim about an observed tax reform.

A different, poorer observation law

Now consider a separate noiseless dataset with only Z varying: P=3+Z/3 and Q=4−2Z/3, generated by demand Q=10−2P and supply Q=c+dP−gZ. For every d>0, choose c=4−3d and g=(2+d)/3. Substitution reproduces every observed (Z,P,Q), so this entire mapping does not identify d. This changes the observation model; it does not preserve the richer W,U,V law above.

With a tax in this supply equation, Q=c+d(P−t)−gZ. At Z=0, Pt=3+dt/(2+d) and Qt=4−2dt/(2+d). The parameter triples (c,d,g)=(1,1,1) and (5/2,1/2,5/6) fit the baseline equally well, but their tax-one outcomes are respectively (10/3,10/3) and (16/5,18/5). Setting g=1 externally forces d=1. That is calibration or additional external information, not identification supplied by the cost-only observations. The empirical task is to justify the exclusions and policy invariance, as well as obtaining informative variation.

3. Minimum distance can estimate a precise approximation

Let m be a k-vector of reported population moments and let Gθ approximate it, with G of full column rank p≤k. For a symmetric positive-definite k×k matrix W, minimize L(θ)=(m−Gθ)′W(m−Gθ) over unrestricted θ∈ℝp. The first-order equation G′WGθ=G′Wm has unique solution θ*=Am, where A=(G′WG)−1G′W. Indeed, G′WG is positive definite since x′G′WGx=(Gx)′W(Gx)>0 for x≠0. Completing the square gives L(θ)=L(θ*)+(θ−θ*)′G′WG(θ−θ*), proving global optimality. A positive residual is entirely compatible with a unique estimator.

Worked case 2: marginal costs and an output prediction

Approximate marginal cost by MC(q)=a+bq; the implied total variable cost is aq+bq²/2. At q=(0,1,2), the reported moments are m=(1,3,6), and W=diag(1,2,1). G has rows (1,0),(1,1),(1,2). Calculation gives

G′WG=((4,4),(4,6)),
A=((3/4,1/2,−1/4),(−1/2,0,1/2)),
(a*,b*)=(3/4,5/2),   m−Gθ*=(1/4,−1/4,1/4),   L(θ*)=1/4.

The successive observed cost increases differ, so no linear marginal-cost curve fits all three moments exactly. θ* is a W-dependent projection. For a separate stipulated sampling law, let m̂N=m+N−1/2ξ with ξ∼N(0,S), S=diag(1,1/2,1). The unrestricted estimator θ̂=A m̂ has an exact Gaussian law with mean θ* and covariance V/N, where

V=ASA′=((3/4,−1/2),(−1/2,1/2)).

This exact linear law does not enforce economic admissibility on every draw. For a locally positive slope b and a price above a, the projection-implied competitive output is q(θ)=(5−a)/b, giving q*=17/10. With b>0 this is the unique maximizer over q≥0 of 5q−aq−bq²/2. Its gradient in (a,b) is (−1/b,−(5−a)/b²); multiplying by A gives its moment sensitivity

∂q/∂m=(1/25,−1/5,−6/25),
√N(q̂−q*) ⇒ N(0,99/1250).

The delta result uses the neighborhood of θ*, where b>0 and price exceeds a, and consistency makes that neighborhood's probability tend to one. One may define a reporting rule outside it without changing this local limit. The unconstrained Gaussian ratio is not a finite-sample normal law, and a denominator that is nonzero almost surely need not give finite ratio moments. Do not label the displayed delta variance an exact finite-sample variance, or report a negative-slope draw as a globally optimal competitive output.

Increase only m₃ by 1/10. Directly re-solving the normal equations gives output 57/34, a change of −2/85. The derivative predicts −3/125. A derivative describes an infinitesimal perturbation; it need not equal a finite difference.

Perfect baseline fit still does not establish extrapolation

In a separate transfer, replace the observed moments by (1,3,5). Both MC₀(q)=1+2q and MC₁(q)=1+2q+q(q−1)(q−2) fit them exactly. Yet MC₁′(q)=1+3(q−1)²>0, so it is a legitimate strictly increasing alternative on q≥0. At price 13, the globally optimal outputs are (6,3). For each model, profit's derivative is price minus marginal cost, positive before its unique crossing and negative after; its integrated cost also dominates revenue at large q. Rank identifies parameters within the chosen linear family. It does not show that family is the true technology outside the observed design points.

4. Specify which simulations share randomness

A simulated model statistic contains additional randomness. Sharing draws across parameter trials can smooth an objective; sharing them across independent observations changes its sampling law. These are different decisions. The scoped Train chapter explains simulated likelihood, moments and scores. The finite constructions here provide their own laws and avoid importing a general simulation asymptotic theorem.

Worked case 3: two kinds of common draws and a wrong likelihood target

Observe Yᵢ=θ₀+εᵢ for i=1,…,N, with independent standard Gaussian εᵢ. A model observation is θ+Zᵢᵣ with standard Gaussian simulation shocks independent of the data. Matching observed and simulated means with R independent draws for every row gives θ̂=Ȳ−(NR)−1ΣᵢᵣZᵢᵣ, exactly normal with variance (1+1/R)/N. Reusing a single set of R shocks in every row instead gives θ̂=Ȳ−R−1ΣᵣZᵣ, with variance 1/N+1/R. At N=100,R=4 these are 1/80 and 13/50. At fixed R, the second estimate tends to the random quantity θ₀−Z̄ as N grows. Additional observations do not average away that common simulation noise.

Now differentiate one R-draw simulator evaluation SR(θ)=θ+Z̄, not an average of N such evaluations. The forward difference [SR(θ+h)−SR(θ)]/h has mean 1 and variance 2/(Rh²) if independent draws are used at the two trial values. With R=4,h=1/100 this is 5000. Reusing exactly the same draws across the two parameter values yields derivative 1 with variance 0. Averaging N independent row differences divides the former variance by N. None of these facts makes a common draw set across all observed rows harmless.

Unbiased probabilities, inconsistent simulated likelihood

For a new iid binary experiment, Yᵢ∼Bernoulli(π), π=9/25. Estimate p∈[1/4,3/4]. Instead of the true model probability p, use p̃ᵢ=p+Zᵢ/5 with independent fair signs Zᵢ, independent of Yᵢ. Then E[p̃ᵢ]=p, and both p̃ᵢ and 1−p̃ᵢ are at least 1/20. Maximize the average simulated log criterion Yᵢ log p̃ᵢ+(1−Yᵢ)log(1−p̃ᵢ).

There are four possible (Y,Z) records. Their empirical frequencies converge to their probabilities, and each log contribution is uniformly bounded and continuous on the compact domain. The supremum difference between the sample criterion and its expectation is bounded by the sum of the four frequency errors times those bounds. This proves a uniform LLN. The population criterion is strictly concave because every individual log contribution has strictly negative second derivative. Its derivative is

Q′(p)=πp/(p²−1/25)−(1−π)(1−p)/((1−p)²−1/25).

At the true probability, Q′(π)=625/1848>0. At p*=2/5 it is zero. Strict concavity establishes the unique interior maximum, and the compact argument establishes convergence to it. The ordinary likelihood instead targets 9/25. The persistent target error is 1/25. Jensen's inequality explains downward bias of the simulated log criterion; solving its expected score establishes the parameter shift. The latter conclusion does not follow from Jensen alone.

Write s=Y/p̃−(1−Y)/(1−p̃). At p*, direct averaging over the four atoms gives H=−E[∂s/∂p]=15/2 and Ω=E[s²]=15/2, since E[s]=0 there. Bounded derivatives give a uniform LLN for the Hessian. Consistency puts the selected maximum in the interior with probability tending to one; Taylor's mean-value identity then gives √N(p̂−p*)=H−1N−1/2Σsᵢ+op(1). The iid finite-support CLT gives asymptotic variance 2/15. The ordinary MLE's variance is 144/625. A smaller variance about the wrong center does not mean better structural estimation.

If p̃ᵢ=p+(1/5)R−1ΣᵣZᵢᵣ, probabilities remain at least 1/20. The derivative of each realized binary log contribution with respect to its probability has absolute value at most 20, so, uniformly in p, its discrepancy from the exact log criterion is at most 4|Z̄ᵢ|. Cauchy–Schwarz gives E|Z̄ᵢ|≤1/√R; averaging rows yields

E[supp|Q̃N,R(p)−QN(p)|]≤4/√R.

Thus RN→∞, Markov's inequality, the ordinary uniform LLN and argmax separation suffice for consistency for π. This is a sufficient consistency argument for this bounded simulator. It does not claim an efficiency rate, an arbitrary log-simulator expansion, or valid dependent-data inference.

5. Auxiliary fit must preserve the joint experiment

Indirect inference estimates a convenient auxiliary statistic or model in the actual data and in data simulated at θ. Its population auxiliary target b(θ) is the binding function. Match those targets, possibly with a positive weight matrix. A many-to-one binding map cannot identify θ globally. Simulation size, common observed inputs and cross covariance all enter the estimator's law. These distinctions are explicit in the inspected theory sections of Gourieroux, Monfort and Renault; their general dependent-process assumptions are not inherited without proof.

Worked case 4: the same covariate in every simulated path

Let Yᵢ=θ₀²+Xᵢ+εᵢ, where Xᵢ and εᵢ are independent standard Gaussian variables, iid across records. Use Θ=[0,3] and the auxiliary sample mean. For each θ simulate Yhᵢ(θ)=θ²+Xᵢ+uhi, h=1,…,H, with fresh independent standard Gaussian u, independent of all actual data, while retaining the same observed Xᵢ in every path and at every θ. The unconditional binding function is b(θ)=θ².

Let ū=(NH)−1Σhiuhi and D=Ȳ−X̄−ū. Minimizing [Ȳ−(θ²+X̄+ū)]² over Θ gives θ̂=√min(9,max(0,D)). The finite synthetic arrays X=(−1,0,1,0), Y=(0,2,4,3), u₁=(−1,0,1,2), u₂=(−1,0,0,1) give Ȳ=9/4, ū=1/4, D=2 and θ̂=sqrt(2). They are a computation example, not purported random evidence about θ₀. On the alternative domain [−3,3], both signs of √2 are global minima; each has a nonzero local derivative b′(θ)=2θ. Local rank does not eliminate the second root.

In the repeated Gaussian experiment, D=θ₀²+ε̄−ū. Consequently √N(D−θ₀²) is exactly N(0,1+1/H). Both the observed and simulated auxiliary means contain X̄. At H=2, their root-N variances and cross covariance are

Var(√NȲ)=2,   Var(√N(X̄+ū))=3/2,
Cov(√NȲ,√N(X̄+ū))=1,   Var(√ND)=3/2.

The covariate contribution cancels. Discarding its covariance would replace 3/2 by 7/2. For 0<θ₀<3 the clipping probability tends to zero, and the identity

θ̂−θ₀=(D−θ₀²)/(θ̂+θ₀)

gives √N(θ̂−θ₀)⇒N(0,(1+1/H)/(4θ₀²)). At θ₀=3/2,H=2 this variance is 1/6; ignoring the cross covariance would give 7/18, and blindly multiplying the observed auxiliary variance by 1+1/H would give 1/3. The last formula is appropriate for a different simulator with independent covariates, not this one.

Consistency does not need a general uniform simulation theorem. The simulated binding differs from θ² by the scalar X̄+ū, independent of θ. Also D→pθ₀². Uniformly for θ∈[0,3], the squared-criterion error is at most |D−θ₀²|(|D−θ₀²|+2θ₀²+18), which vanishes. Injectivity on the nonnegative compact domain and the separation argument apply, including the boundary.

At θ₀=0, however, the derivative vanishes. Write Z=√ND∼N(0,3/2). Apart from upper clipping whose probability vanishes, N1/4θ̂=√max(Z,0). The limit is nonnormal with probability 1/2 at zero. At θ₀=3, upper clipping instead invalidates the interior Gaussian law, as exercise 8 shows. Identification, consistency and regular root-N inference are separate statements.

6. Solve and differentiate the mechanism inside the criterion

The nested fixed-point idea solves the agent's dynamic problem at each trial parameter and then evaluates the data likelihood. The inspected Rust article is a primary example. Its empirical estimates and general companion-paper theorems are not used here. We state the shock normalization explicitly and prove a finite two-state model.

Why centered Gumbel shocks produce log-sum values

Let independent ηj have CDF F(x)=exp(−exp(−x)). Its mean μ exists: for t≥0, P(η>t)≤e−t, and P(η<−t)=exp(−et) is integrable. Define εj=ηj−μ. For finite deterministic indices zj, independence gives

P(maxj(zj+ηj)≤x)=exp(−e−xΣjezj)=F(x−log Σjezj).

Taking expectations and subtracting μ yields E maxj(zj+εj)=log Σezj. No numerical Euler constant or ambiguous sign is required. Integrating the density of ηj against the other CDFs, with substitution w=e−ηj, gives the unique-choice probability ezj/Σezk; ties have probability zero. Common centering changes the value level but not these probabilities.

Log-sum-exp is monotone and satisfies L(z+k1)=L(z)+k. If max|z−z̃|≤e, sandwiching between z̃−e1 and z̃+e1 proves |L(z)−L(z̃)|≤e. With stochastic transition rows and a discount 0≤β<1, continuation indices change by at most β‖V−Ṽ‖∞. Thus the Bellman operator T is a β-contraction. Iterated differences decay geometrically, the iterates form a Cauchy sequence in a finite-dimensional complete space, continuity makes its limit a fixed point, and the contraction makes two fixed points impossible. For any proposed Ṽ,

‖Ṽ−V*‖∞≤δ/(1−β),   δ=‖TṼ−Ṽ‖∞.

This certificate concerns the supplied model. It neither identifies its parameters nor proves its behavioral assumptions.

Worked case 5: replacement, a maintained discount and a subsidy

The state s is 0 or 1. Keeping the asset gives deterministic utility −cs and moves to state 1 with probability one. Replacing gives utility −r and moves to state 0. The two centered choice shocks have the law above, independent across alternatives and dates. Each fresh shock vector is independent of past information and the predetermined current state. The decision maker observes the current state and both current shocks before choosing; future shocks are unobserved. The current choice determines the next state. The objective is expected discounted utility with known 0≤β<1. Before the current shocks are realized,

(TV)s=log[exp(−cs+βV₁)+exp(−r+βV₀)],
ps=P(replace|s)=exp(−r+βV₀)/(exp(−cs+βV₁)+exp(−r+βV₀)).

Why this fixed point is the optimization value. An admissible policy uses past information, the current state and current shocks, but not future shocks. Let u(s,a) denote the deterministic payoff and let C=maxs,a|u(s,a)|+E[maxa|εa|], which is finite by the finite state/action sets and the Gumbel tail bounds. Under every such policy, the expected absolute discounted payoff after period H−1 is at most CβH/(1−β), uniformly over initial states. With zero terminal continuation, backward induction gives the H-period optimal value TH0: after observing the current shocks one chooses the larger payoff-plus-continuation index, and independent future shocks give the next pre-shock value. Truncating any infinite policy, or extending any finite policy, changes its expected value by at most this tail bound. Thus finite-horizon optimal values converge uniformly to the infinite-horizon supremum. Contraction also gives TH0→V*, so this supremum equals the fixed point.

Choose at each date the action maximizing u(s,a)+εa+βV*(next state). This is a measurable stationary rule, with ties of probability zero. Iterating its conditional Bellman equality for H periods yields V*(s₀)=E[Σt=0H−1βt(u(st,at)+εt,a_t)+βHV*(sH)]. The terminal term tends to zero because V* is bounded on the finite state space; the same absolute-tail bound justifies passage to the infinite payoff sum. This rule therefore attains the stated optimum. The conclusion uses the information and shock law just specified, not contraction alone.

Take β=1/2, r=log 5 and c=log(20/11). Direct substitution verifies

V*=(0,log(16/25)),   (p₀,p₁)=(1/5,5/16).

At state 0 the two exponentials are 4/5 and 1/5; at state 1 they are 11/25 and 1/5. Their sums are 1 and 16/25. Contraction turns this verification into a uniqueness proof. Under the stationary policy, the controlled transition matrix and its invariant distribution are

Pπ=((1/5,4/5),(5/16,11/16)),   ρ=(25/89,64/89).

Solve ρ₀=ρ₀p₀+(1−ρ₀)p₁ to obtain the distribution; both transition columns are positive, and the scalar stationary equation has a unique solution. The stationary replacement rate is 25/89, because replacement determines next period's state 0. This calculation does not justify an iid likelihood for a trajectory.

The observation law matters

Our likelihood uses 36 independent decision makers observed once: 20 are initialized in state 0, with 4 replacements; 16 are initialized in state 1, with 5 replacements. Initial states are fixed by this synthetic design. These are not consecutive decisions from one asset. Conditional on those states, the individual-decision product likelihood has log value

4 log p₀+16 log(1−p₀)+5 log p₁+11 log(1−p₁)=−19.945430463648.

An aggregate binomial likelihood adds parameter-independent combinatorial terms; the displayed individual-record convention omits them. Each group likelihood is strictly concave in its own probability and maximized at its observed fraction. For a genuine trajectory conditional on its initial state, the likelihood instead factors sequentially as Πtp(at|st)P(st+1|st,at). A path incompatible with the deterministic transitions has probability zero. Conditioning each action on the complete future state path is a different experiment, since future states reveal information about earlier actions. No trajectory CLT is claimed here.

What the two probabilities identify

For positive probabilities below one, define ks=log((1−ps)/ps) and Δ=V₁−V₀. Because the replacement index is identical in both states, p₀/p₁=eΔ. Also ks=r−cs+βΔ. Therefore

Δ=log(p₀/p₁),   c=k₀−k₁,   r=k₀−βΔ,
V₀=(−r−log p₀)/(1−β),   V₁=V₀+Δ.

These identities give an inverse on the admissible model domain. Our fitted fractions yield positive r,c. A pair of probabilities implying negative c would fail a restriction c≥0, rather than identifying a positive deterioration cost. With β known and the stated location/scale normalization, the two rates identify r,c. If β is unknown, the family c=k₀−k₁ and r(β)=k₀−βΔ fits exactly for every admissible β; observing fit does not identify patience or the absolute utility scale.

Differentiate the solved model

The derivative of T with respect to V is βPπ. For j∈{r,c}, differentiate the fixed-point equation to get (I−βPπ)Vj=gj, where gr=−(p₀,p₁)′ and gc=(0,−(1−p₁))′. The inverse exists: its Neumann series Σk≥0βkPπk converges in sup norm, since stochastic rows give ‖Pπk‖∞=1. Smooth finite log-sum functions and this nonsingular derivative justify the local implicit derivative. At the stated parameters, with rows indexed by states and columns by (r,c),

∂V/∂(r,c)=((−82/169,−88/169),(−100/169,−198/169)),
∂log(p/(1−p))/∂(r,c)=((−160/169,55/169),(−160/169,224/169)),
∂p/∂(r,c)=((−128/845,44/845),(−275/1352,385/1352)).

The log odds equal −r+cs+β(V₀−V₁), and multiplying their derivatives by ps(1−ps) gives the last matrix. Holding V fixed would incorrectly give log-odds derivatives (−1,s); it ignores how future options change with current primitives.

A maintained subsidy adds log 2 utility units to replacement, so r falls by log 2. Re-solving the Bellman equation at β=1/2 gives replacement probabilities (0.324103368522,0.465768472136). The observationally equivalent static baseline β=0,r=log 4,c unchanged gives the same original probabilities but, after the same utility subsidy, gives (1/3,10/21). Baseline fit does not identify this policy response when the discount factor is free. Nor is a normalized utility subsidy an identified dollar payment or welfare benefit.

Carry numerical accuracy into the likelihood

If Ṽ has Bellman residual δ, every choice index changes by at most βδ/(1−β), and its log-sum denominator changes by at most the same amount. Thus the absolute log probability error for either choice is at most 2βδ/(1−β). An average log likelihood obeys the same bound; the sum over N records obeys N times it. Numerical error, simulation error and sampling uncertainty are separate quantities. As β approaches 1, even this finite model's worst-case value-error amplification deteriorates. A small residual is not a confidence interval, and a successful inner solve is not a proof of an outer optimum or parameter identification.

7. A unique numerical answer may hide a selection assumption

Worked case 6: adoption with strategic complementarity

A unit mass of agents has an exactly specified logistic taste distribution F(x)=Λ(x)=1/(1+e−x). An agent with taste threshold τ adopts when τ≤a+bq, taking aggregate adoption q as given. The distribution itself supplies the population fraction Λ(a+bq); no continuum iid law is invoked. Equilibrium satisfies q=Λ(a+bq). Both parameters and any policy h below are in the normalized taste-index units.

The response is continuous and maps [0,1] into (0,1), so its difference from q changes sign at the endpoints; the intermediate-value theorem gives an equilibrium. Since Λ′=Λ(1−Λ)≤1/4, |b|<4 gives a contraction and uniqueness. For example b=2,a=−1 gives unique q=1/2, contraction modulus 1/2 and dq/da=1/2.

Now take b=4 log 3 and a=−2 log 3=−b/2. An intervention adds h to a, preserving b and the taste law. For q∈(0,1), define F(q)=log(q/(1−q))−b(q−1/2). The equilibrium equation is F(q)=h. At h=0, the three exact roots are (1/4,1/2,3/4). To prove these are all roots, observe F′(q)=1/[q(1−q)]−b. Since b>4, it vanishes only at

q−=(1−√(1−4/b))/2,   q+=(1+√(1−4/b))/2,
(q−,q+)≈(0.350199488174,0.649800511826).

F is strictly increasing, then strictly decreasing, then strictly increasing on the intervals separated by q−,q+, with endpoint limits −∞ and +∞. It has at most three roots for any h; the three exact baseline roots therefore exhaust them. Symmetry gives F(1−q)=−F(q). Let h*=F(q−)=0.040128279987, a positive local maximum, and F(q+)=−h*. There are three distinct equilibria for |h|<h*, two distinct equilibria at |h|=h* with one tangent root, and one for |h|>h*. The tangent is a genuine fold since F″(q)=−(1−2q)/[q²(1−q)²] is nonzero at q− and q+.

Off a fold, implicit differentiation gives dq/dh=q(1−q)/[1−bq(1−q)]. At the three baseline roots the derivatives are (1.065094100772,−2.535180993937,1.065094100772). The negative derivative of the middle branch does not identify the aggregate response to a policy with unspecified selection. At a fold the denominator is zero and the regular derivative argument fails.

For the specifically declared iteration qn+1=Λ(a+h+bqn), the local slopes at baseline are (0.823959216501,1.098612288668,0.823959216501). By continuity of the derivative, a sufficiently small neighborhood contracts around either outer root; the middle root locally expands deviations. These are stability statements about this iteration. They do not establish that actual agents or a market use that adjustment rule, and a slope equal to one at a fold cannot be classified by the strict linear contraction test.

Bisection on the three monotone intervals gives, at h=0.02, roots (0.276055632624,0.447304640831,0.768539867449); at h=0.1 there is the unique root 0.815631673251. The numerical brackets locate roots; the shape proof establishes the complete count. Continuing a selected low branch requires an explicit branch-continuation rule, and that branch disappears at h*. Observing a low baseline equilibrium does not establish how the market selects after this disappearance.

With unrestricted randomized equilibrium selection at h=0.02, the mean outcome can be any point in (0.276055632624,0.768539867449), interpreted as the endpoints of a closed interval. Every interior mean is generated by an appropriate mixture of the extreme roots; every mixture lies between them. A realized equilibrium still lies in the three-point root set. This interval describes unidentified selection, not sampling uncertainty or a confidence interval. A policy claim needs either a scientifically defended selection rule or an explicit report of this remaining set.

8. A reproducible structural argument

Begin with the observable records and their law. Specify θ, its domain, maintained normalizations, which quantities are calibrated, and which variation identifies each parameter. Derive the map or identified set before interpreting an optimizer. Then state the intervention and exactly which primitives and selection rule stay fixed.

Keep three errors visible. Sampling error comes from the actual data law. Simulation error comes from the number and coupling of artificial draws. Numerical approximation comes from stopping an optimization, discretizing a state space or solving a fixed point incompletely. Increasing one budget need not reduce the other errors. Independent redraws at each parameter trial can obscure a derivative; fixing one draw set for all observed rows can leave nonvanishing noise; an accurately solved wrong model can produce a precise wrong policy answer.

Audit alternate parameter vectors, admissible domains, moment weights, simulation sharing, discount factors and equilibrium branches. Report which conclusions survive those interventions. The checker reconstructs this chapter's finite contracts with standard-library arithmetic, exact fractions and bounded root calculations; it does not fit a real economic dataset or certify empirical invariance.

9. Exercises

  1. In case 1, verify the reduced form and use Z to identify demand's price coefficient and W to identify supply's coefficient. Replace the demand instrument by T=Z+U. Compute its covariance ratio Cov(T,Q)/Cov(T,P), and explain precisely which identifying restriction fails.
  2. In the separate noiseless cost-only case, prove that c=4−3d and g=(2+d)/3 give the same observed mapping for every d>0. Calculate the tax-one (P,Q) at Z=0 when d=2. If external evidence fixes g=5/6, what d and tax-one prediction result? Explain why the richer experiment and calibration must not be conflated.
  3. For case 2, change W to the identity while retaining m=(1,3,6). Derive the unique projection, its price-five output and the weighted loss under this new criterion. Explain why changing a weight can change a pseudo-true parameter, and why neither an exact Gaussian parameter law nor a nonzero ratio denominator proves a finite-sample Gaussian output law.
  4. In the perfect-fit transfer, define MCκ(q)=1+2q+κq(q−1)(q−2) for 0≤κ≤1. Prove all these curves fit q=0,1,2 and are strictly increasing on q≥0. At price 13 prove the global optimum is unique and lies in [3,6]. Derive dq/dκ and evaluate it at κ=1. State what the observed fit leaves unidentified.
  5. For the additive Gaussian simulator, derive the independent-row and common-row estimator variances, then calculate both at N=80,R=5. For one R-draw simulator evaluated at two parameter values separated by h=1/50, calculate the forward-difference variance with independent draws and with common draws. State the fixed-R probability limit in the common-row design.
  6. Keep the one-sign binary simulator and compact p domain, but change the true probability to π=1/2. Prove its pseudo-true maximizer is now 1/2 despite strict Jensen bias in the criterion. Derive dp*/dπ at π=1/2 and the estimator's root-N variance there. Does a variance below the ordinary MLE's contradict an efficiency bound for regular estimation of π? Also prove the original growing-R consistency bound and identify the uniform-convergence step.
  7. In case 4, replace every retained Xᵢ in the simulations by a fresh independent standard Gaussian Xhi, independent across h,i and of all data and u. At H=2 and θ₀=3/2 derive the auxiliary difference variance and θ estimator's asymptotic variance. Compare with shared X, showing which cross covariance changes.
  8. For the original shared-X case with H=2, derive the estimator on [0,3], the sign-unrestricted minimizers for the supplied arrays, and the nonnormal limits at θ₀=0 and θ₀=3. Prove consistency using an actual uniform criterion bound and the compact separation argument. Explain why nonzero local rank and global identification are different.
  9. Derive the centered-Gumbel expected maximum and softmax probability from its CDF. If a common constant κ is added to every period's shock, prove the effect on the Bellman value and on the choices. For β=0.9 and an approximate value with residual δ=0.001, give the value-error bound, per-record log-probability bound and 36-record summed bound. State what fails in this proof at β=1.
  10. Starting with the observed replacement fractions, derive the inverse formulas for Δ,c,r and the whole baseline-equivalent family indexed by β∈[0,1). At β=1/2 derive the c column of the value and probability derivatives, and contrast it with holding V fixed. Explain the observation-law requirement for the supplied likelihood and why the two subsidy predictions cannot identify dollar welfare.
  11. Prove the complete equilibrium count for every h in case 6, including the folds. Use symmetry to give the roots for h=−0.02. Identify the stable branches for the stated iteration at baseline, and state the randomized-selection mean interval at h=−0.02. Distinguish this interval from the realized equilibrium set and from a confidence interval.
  12. A report claims: “The optimizer converged, simulated moments fit, and one equilibrium solver returned a point. Therefore the primitive parameters and policy effect are identified; increasing the simulation budget makes our confidence interval cover all model uncertainty.” Write an audit response using at least three chapter cases. Specify an identification check, a justified sampling or simulation law, a numerical certificate and an explicit policy-invariance or selection condition. Give a useful conclusion that can still be reported if one condition fails.
Complete solutions, proofs and evaluation criteria

  1. Equating the two equations gives 3P=9+W+Z+U−V; substitution yields the displayed Q. Independence of the four centered signs and unit variances give Cov(Z,P)=1/3, Cov(Z,Q)=−2/3 and Cov(W,P)=Cov(W,Q)=1/3. The two ratios are (−2,1). For T=Z+U, Cov(T,P)=2/3 and Cov(T,Q)=−1/3, giving −1/2. Relevance survives, but Cov(T,U)=1, violating the demand disturbance orthogonality. A strong first stage alone does not establish an instrument's exclusion/exogeneity.

  2. Substituting P=3+Z/3 into supply gives c+3d+(d/3−g)Z=4−2Z/3 exactly when c=4−3d and g=(2+d)/3. Demand also holds identically. Under the tax, equating 10−2P=c+d(P−1) at Z=0 gives P=3+d/(2+d), Q=4−2d/(2+d). At d=2 these are (7/2,3). External g=5/6 implies d=3g−2=1/2, giving (16/5,18/5). The family reproduces the cost-only law, not the original joint W,U,V experiment. Fixing g supplies information absent from that law; it cannot be relabeled an estimate from its identifying variation.

  3. The new normal matrix is [[3,3],[3,5]], with determinant 6>0, and G′m=(10,15)′. Solving gives (a,b)=(5/6,5/2), residuals (1/6,−1/3,1/6), and sum of squares 1/6. The price-five output is 5/3. The positive-definite completed square proves uniqueness. When the model cannot fit all moments, changing W changes which errors are penalized, hence the projection target. Exact linear transformation preserves Gaussianity for (â,b̂), but division by b̂ is nonlinear and can have heavy tails near zero. The delta law is a local asymptotic statement around b*>0; finite-sample normality and finite ratio moments require separate arguments.

  4. The added cubic vanishes at 0,1,2. Its derivative yields MCκ′=2−κ+3κ(q−1)²≥1, establishing strict increase. MCκ(3)=7+6κ≤13 and MCκ(6)=13+120κ≥13, so continuity and monotonicity give exactly one price-13 crossing in [3,6]. Integrated costs grow at least quadratically; profit rises before the crossing and falls after it, proving the global optimum over q≥0. Implicit differentiation gives dq/dκ=−q(q−1)(q−2)/[2−κ+3κ(q−1)²]. At κ=1, q=3 and the derivative is −6/13. The three design points leave κ, extrapolated marginal costs and the resulting policy output unidentified. A within-family rank calculation cannot choose κ.

  5. Independent data and simulations give Var(Ȳ−Z̄NR)=1/N+1/(NR); a shared R-draw set gives 1/N+1/R. At the new inputs the variances are (3/200,17/80). Independently redrawing the two simulator values gives variance (1/R+1/R)/h²=1000. Identical draws cancel, leaving derivative 1 and variance 0. At fixed R, the shared-row estimator converges conditional on its simulation draws to θ₀−Z̄R, a random quantity unconditionally. The effect of reusing draws across parameter trials is therefore different from reusing them across records.

  6. At π=1/2 the expected criterion is symmetric under p↦1−p and strictly concave, so its unique maximizer is 1/2. The log is strictly concave and the simulated probability is nonconstant, so Jensen bias remains strict; symmetry prevents a target shift at this one truth. At p*=1/2 the two simulated probabilities are 3/10 and 7/10. Averaging the four scores gives H=Ω=2900/441. The expected score's derivative in π is 1/(3/10)+1/(7/10)=100/21. Implicit differentiation of the expected score zero gives dp*/dπ=21/29; the sandwich variance is 441/2900, below 1/4. This procedure is not regular, locally consistent estimation of π in a neighborhood: its target responds at 21/29 instead of 1. Indeed p*(1/2+δ)=1/2+(21/29)δ+o(δ), so for nearby fixed truths the estimator converges to the wrong probability. Its smaller pointwise variance is not a comparison of procedures that regularly estimate the same structural target throughout a neighborhood.

    For R signs, all probabilities stay in [1/20,19/20]. A log contribution is 20-Lipschitz on that interval; multiplying by |Z̄|/5 gives discrepancy ≤4|Z̄|. Taking the supremum before averaging can only increase the bound, and E|Z̄|≤√E[Z̄²]=1/√R. Thus E sup|Q̃−Q|≤4/√R. Markov's inequality makes it vanish in probability when R→∞. The exact binary likelihood has a uniform LLN by its two empirical frequencies and compact bounded logs. Together with unique population maximization at π, compact separation establishes consistency. No unproved pointwise-to-uniform step or efficiency rate is needed.

  7. The actual auxiliary mean still has root-N variance 2. The simulated mean now averages H independent copies of X+u, so its root-N variance is 2/H=1 at H=2, and its cross covariance with the observed mean is zero. The difference variance is 3. Dividing by (2θ₀)²=9 gives parameter variance 1/3. Retaining X instead gives covariance 1 and difference variance 3/2, hence 1/6. The sample law changed, so its covariance formula must change. Reusing the same observed path is not equivalent to simulating an independent path with the same marginal distribution.

  8. Writing z=θ² maps [0,3] bijectively to [0,9]; projection of D onto that interval gives θ̂=√min(9,max(0,D)). The supplied arrays give D=2, so the alternative sign domain has minimizers (−sqrt(2),sqrt(2)). At θ₀=0, Z=√ND has exact law N(0,3/2), giving N1/4θ̂⇒√max(Z,0), with atom 1/2 at zero. At θ₀=3, write D=9+Z/√N. Negative Z gives √N(√D−3)=Z/(√D+3)→Z/6, and positive Z is clipped to zero. Hence √N(θ̂−3)⇒min(Z/6,0), again with atom 1/2 at zero. Neither boundary has the interior Gaussian law.

    For all θ∈[0,3], the absolute difference between (θ²−D)² and (θ²−θ₀²)² is bounded by |D−θ₀²|(|D−θ₀²|+2θ₀²+18). The known Gaussian law makes this bound converge to zero in probability. The population criterion is continuous with a unique minimum on the nonnegative domain, so apply the section 1 separation proof to its negative. On the sign-unrestricted domain the two roots violate uniqueness even though b′ is nonzero at either nonzero root. At zero, global identification on [0,3] holds while local derivative rank fails.

  9. Multiplying the CDFs gives a standard Gumbel variable shifted by log Σezj; subtracting its common finite mean leaves precisely that expected maximum. For choice j, integrate f(x)Πk≠jF(x+zj−zk) dx. Substituting w=e−x yields ∫₀∞exp[−wΣkexp(zk−zj)]dw=ezj/Σezk. A common period shock shift κ changes T to T+κ. Translation of continuation values verifies Vnew=V*+κ/(1−β); every action index changes by the same κ+βκ/(1−β), so choices do not change. Contraction proves that shifted value is unique.

    The supplied residual gives value error at most 1/100, log-probability error at most 9/500 per record, and summed error at most 81/125. At β=1 the geometric bound and Neumann series no longer converge. Translation has modulus one; existence, uniqueness and error control require a different undiscounted theory, and cannot be inherited from this proof.

  10. The common replacement index gives p₀/p₁=exp(V₁−V₀), so Δ=log(16/25). The keep-to-replace log odds satisfy ks=r−cs+βΔ. Thus c=k₀−k₁=log(20/11), while r(β)=log 4−β log(16/25). Substituting V₀=(−r−log p₀)/(1−β) and V₁=V₀+Δ verifies the Bellman equations and the same two baseline rates for every β∈[0,1); r,c stay positive. This is observational equivalence with two one-choice probabilities, not an identified discount factor.

    At β=1/2, solve (I−βPπ)Vc=(0,−11/16)′ to get Vc=(−88/169,−198/169). The log-odds derivatives are (55/169,224/169), and probability derivatives are (44/845,385/1352). Holding V fixed would give log-odds derivatives (0,1), missing both continuation effects. The data likelihood requires independent, once-observed decision makers with the stated initial states. A single path needs sequential action/transition factors. Finally the subsidy is specified in normalized utility units with no money-to-utility coefficient or welfare aggregation supplied; differing predictions under equivalent β do not identify dollar welfare.

  11. F′ has exactly the two critical points q−,q+, with signs +,−,+ and infinite endpoint limits. F(q−)=h*>0 and F(q+)=−h*, proving the three/two/one count for |h| below/equal/above h*. The nonzero F″ at the critical points proves tangency rather than a locally constant segment. Symmetry gives the h=−0.02 roots by reversing and subtracting the positive-policy roots from one: (0.231460132551,0.552695359169,0.723944367376). The outer baseline branches attract under the declared naive iteration since their slope magnitudes are below one; the middle repels since its slope exceeds one. This does not supply an empirical selection law. Randomized-selection means fill the closed interval with endpoints (0.231460132551,0.723944367376); individual realized equilibria remain the three roots. These are model selection possibilities, not probability coverage for a sampled estimator.

  12. A strong response separates the claims. Case 1 exhibits the same cost-only observables with different tax incidence; the richer instrument experiment identifies slopes only under its exclusions. Case 2 has a unique full-rank minimum-distance target without exact structural fit, and its perfect-fit alternatives disagree outside observed quantities. Case 3 shows that a shared draw set can survive an infinite data sample and that an unbiased probability simulator can target the wrong likelihood parameter. Case 4 requires cross covariance and distinguishes global signs from local rank. Case 5 supplies a valid inner residual certificate but leaves β unidentifiable from the two rates, and case 6 requires an equilibrium-selection rule.

    Evaluation criteria. An adequate audit gives (i) a concrete observable-map or excluded-variation check with its maintained restrictions; (ii) an explicit actual/simulated joint law and an inference result whose regularity conditions hold; (iii) a numerical certificate such as residual/(1−β), with the criterion convention identified; and (iv) a policy invariance or selection condition that fit alone cannot establish. It supports at least three points with specific cases rather than labels. A useful restricted report can give a pseudo-target with correct sampling uncertainty, a set of policy predictions across admissible primitives or selections, or a numerical approximation bound without claiming identification. Increasing simulation size does not eliminate misspecification, missing instruments, unknown selection or invalid confidence coverage. Independent empirical and substantive evaluation remains necessary.

10. Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain to an analyst why “the model fits and the solver converged” does not identify a policy response. Use a model-to-data map, one numerical certificate and one observationally equivalent alternative. Benchmark answer. In the dynamic case, known β and normalized shocks map (r,c) into two choice rates; a small Bellman residual bounds value and log-likelihood error for each trial. But changing β and r together preserves those rates while changing the subsidy response. The solver certifies an inner calculation, while identification and policy invariance need separate evidence. A clear explanation specifies which uncertainty each statement addresses.

Retention check. Without notes, distinguish global identification from local rank; write the shared-X covariance subtraction; state why centering the Gumbel leaves log-sum expected values; and identify the failed denominator at a fold. Answers. θ and −θ can share a squared binding value despite nonzero derivatives. The difference variance is Var(A)+Var(B)−2Cov(A,B); the shared X cancels. The maximum of shifted standard Gumbels is distributed as a standard Gumbel plus log-sum-exp, so subtracting its mean removes the constant. At a fold 1−bq(1−q)=0, invalidating the regular implicit derivative. Re-derive one of these results a week later with changed domain or simulation sharing, rather than memorizing its numerical value.

The next chapter develops Bayesian, high-dimensional and machine-learning methods. Alternative inference and flexible prediction tools still require a defined target, a justified observation law, controlled computation and a defensible policy interpretation.

Sources and further study

  • Kenneth Train — Discrete Choice Methods with Simulation, second edition, Chapter 10: Simulation-Assisted Estimation — Scope-limited method context for simulation-assisted criteria, distinct simulation bias/noise and simulation design; original finite proofs must supply their own conditions.
  • John Rust — Optimal Replacement of GMC Bus Engines: An Empirical Model of Harold Zurcher — Scope-limited primary example of dynamic structural primitives, reduced Bellman/choice construction and nested fixed-point estimation; original finite-state proofs and normalization are separate.
  • Christian Gourieroux, Alain Monfort, Eric Renault — Indirect Inference — Primary binding-function and indirect minimum-distance framework with explicit injectivity/rank, simulation and covariance assumptions; original bounded inference must be proved independently.
